The conservative parliament speaker-turned-negotiator is under major pressure over his efforts to reach a deal with the US to end the war.

The source continued, “Rezaee has a strong tendency to seek dominance. Combined with his perception that Qalibaf and others have historically been subordinate to him, this could create a significant obstacle for both Qalibaf and Reformist President Masoud Pezeshkian, who are seeking to build an internal consensus in Iran around reaching a deal with US President Donald Trump,” the source explained, adding, “This is while Mohammad Baqer Zolqadr, the dismissed previous secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, was a close friend and ally of Qalibaf.”

All in all, the broader picture is increasingly clear: Khamenei’s appointments do not necessarily represent the beginning of a new Iranian military doctrine. Instead, they appear to reflect the positions and ambitions of competing factions, networks of power and personalities that have been fighting for influence for years.

What may on the surface seem like a series of routine personnel changes may, in reality, be the early stage of a much larger struggle over who controls Iran’s security apparatus—and ultimately, who gets to shape the post-Ali Khamenei order.

Here's an infographic we shared with clients a couple of days ago for folks to understand. The maths are quite simple.

Our method is to count the daily average of what departs the US Navy blockade line. We then substract from that what we know comes out of Oman and Fujairah. The rest is traffic deriving via the Strait of Hormuz.

Equation: USN - Oman - Fuj= SoH.

The Ship-to-Ship transfers happen in the Gulf of Oman west of the USN blockade line. Once the STS is done, the receiving party then departs via the USN blockade line. And that's where we count the regional departures.

That's the number that ulitimately moves oil markets.

https://t.co/chY9tBSS66 counts shipments to the global market when they pass through the US blockade line, monitoring the Automatic Identification System signals of ships because of restrictions on timely satellite imagery. On that basis, flows over the past seven days stand at just 3.7 million barrels a day, Samir Madani, the firm’s co-founder says.

https://t.co/WuHSxD5NDz
That's 3.7 Mbpd via the SoH and not the blockade line. If you add the exports out of Fujairah, UAE and Oman, it's slightly over 6 Mbpd.

Ever since China slapped on rare earth export curbs following the Spring '25 Liberation Day tariff shock, physical flows of Chinese rare earths and permanent magnets haven't mounted any real recovery.

#Wheat: Before the latest 8% surge in CBOT wheat, driven by mounting supply concerns as the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted exports from a region that in a normal year accounts for more than 25% of global wheat exports, it is worth noting that wheat was one of just three BCOM commodities in which managed money still held a net short position.

Speculators have maintained a net short in CBOT wheat for most of the period since 2022, encouraged not only by a comfortable supply outlook but also by an elevated contango. A contango market provides a positive carry for short sellers when they roll a position from a lower-priced nearby contract into a higher-priced deferred contract. As recently as May, the one-year contango was around 12%, implying that, at an unchanged prompt price, a short position could earn roughly 12% over a year simply from the roll.

That dynamic is now changing. As the supply outlook tightens, the one-year contango has narrowed to below 5%, significantly reducing the carry incentive for maintaining a short position. Combined with rising prices, this increases the pressure on existing shorts to cover.

With that in mind, any further deterioration in the supply outlook could see the rally amplified by a shift in speculative positioning from short covering towards outright net-long exposure - something managed money has not held in earnest for more than four years.

#Agriculture: Wheat futures in Chicago hit a three-year high as concerns grow that the war between Russia and Ukraine could escalate further and disrupt supplies from a region that accounts for more than 25% of global wheat exports. Ukraine is already facing a drop of more than 50% in agricultural exports this season compared with previous estimates, according to its agriculture ministry. Meanwhile, Russia’s wheat shipments are expected to fall by more than 50% in August from a year earlier. Overall, these developments are squeezing farmer cash flow, potentially affecting planting and next year’s production.
#CrudeOil prices rebounded strongly on Wednesday, with Brent rising from below USD 86 to near USD 90 on reports of a potential Russian escalation in Ukraine, before reversing on news of an Iranian revenue-sharing agreement covering shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Prices are down around 8% from Monday’s peak amid renewed Middle East supply optimism, while US inventory data highlighted continued stress in refined products, with gasoline stocks falling to their lowest seasonal level since 2012 and diesel inventories to a record low, just ahead of the winter demand season.
#Gold continues to consolidate following last week’s surge, with prices so far finding support below USD 4,600, ahead of the USD 4,555 level, the 0.382 Fibonacci retracement of the latest rally. Attention is now turning to Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech at the Jackson Hole symposium tomorrow, with markets looking for further guidance on the interest-rate outlook and how policymakers view the balance between inflation, growth and financial conditions. Following the latest inflation print, one full 25-basis-point hike is now priced by December.

Takeaways from the latest EIA inventory report:

US crude stocks rose less than expected, while Cushing inventories continued to recover. A further 3.7 million barrels were released from the SPR, taking the total draw to 125 million barrels, a 30% reduction. Both exports and imports slowed, leaving the net impact broadly unchanged.

Refinery utilisation jumped to its highest seasonal level since 1998 as record-high refining margins incentivised production amid strong export demand due to Russian export ban and stranded capacity in the Persian Gulf.

Gasoline stocks fell to their lowest seasonal level since 2012 at 209.4 million barrels, while distillate inventories plunged to a record low of 105.6 million barrels.

Implied gasoline demand held steady on a four-week average basis, while distillate demand strengthened.
